why_how.text: Points track risky driving over time, so DMV can step in with a clinic before suspending a license.
The thresholds tighten after a reinstatement, because a driver who has already been suspended gets less room the second time.

scenario.text: Quinn has eight points after two convictions in eighteen months, and DMV sends a clinic notice.

reasoning.text: At seven points DMV may require the driver improvement clinic, and satisfactorily finishing it removes three points.

result.text: Quinn completes the clinic and drops to five points, further from the twelve-point suspension threshold.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the twelve-point suspension threshold applies again after a reinstatement.

correction.text: After reinstatement, only eight points within three years can bring a second suspension.

prompt.text: Quinn has eight points and finishes the driver improvement clinic. How many points remain?

answer.text: Five points, because the clinic removes three.

rationale.text: Satisfactorily finishing the clinic takes three points off the record.

narration.text: This chapter is about losing, and getting back, the privilege to drive. It starts with the point system. Being convicted of certain motor vehicle violations in North Carolina puts driver license points on your record, and as those points add up, DMV can take action. In this lesson you will learn the three numbers that matter most: the point total that can send you to a driver improvement clinic, the total that can lead to a suspension, and the lower total that applies after a license has already been reinstated. You will also learn what the clinic does for your record.

Once you reach seven points, DMV may send you to a driver improvement clinic, and the clinic costs eighty-three dollars and fifty cents. The clinic is a warning and a chance to improve before anything worse happens. Finishing the driver improvement clinic satisfactorily takes three points off your record. So a driver at eight points who completes the clinic drops to five. Think of the clinic as an early off-ramp. It does not erase the record, but it pulls the total back from the suspension line, and it teaches habits that keep new points from piling on.

lines.text: After reinstatement: eight in three years.

narration.text: Collecting twelve points within three years can get your license suspended. That is the first suspension threshold. After the license is reinstated, the threshold drops. Gathering eight points within the next three years can bring a second suspension. The three-year window applies in both cases, so points do not count against you forever, but they do accumulate over a fairly long stretch. A few moving violations, each worth three or four points, can reach these totals faster than most drivers expect, which is why the clinic warning at seven points deserves attention.

Here is the trap. Three point totals sit close together, and practice questions shuffle them. Seven points can send you to a driver improvement clinic. Twelve points within three years can cost you the license. And after reinstatement, only eight points within three years can bring a second suspension. A common wrong answer applies twelve again after a reinstatement, or treats seven as a suspension. Keep the order with the memory line: seven clinic, twelve, then eight. The clinic comes first, the first suspension at twelve, and the tighter second threshold at eight.

Here is a quick check: Quinn has collected eight points over eighteen months and receives a notice to attend the driver improvement clinic. Quinn completes the clinic satisfactorily. How many points remain on Quinn's record? Work it out before reading on. The answer is five points. Satisfactorily finishing the driver improvement clinic takes three points off your record, and eight minus three is five. That moves Quinn further from the twelve-point suspension threshold. The clinic does not wipe the record clean; only reinstatement after a suspension does that, as the next lesson explains.

Let us pull this together. Being convicted of certain motor vehicle violations puts driver license points on your North Carolina record. At seven points DMV may send you to a driver improvement clinic, which costs eighty-three dollars and fifty cents, and finishing it satisfactorily takes three points off. Twelve points within three years can get your license suspended. After reinstatement, eight points within the next three years can bring a second suspension. Next, we look at how long point suspensions last and what reinstatement does to your points.

why_how.text: Suspensions grow longer with each repeat, so a pattern of violations costs more each time.
Reinstatement clears license points, but insurers track their own points, so the money side of a bad record lingers.

scenario.text: Drew's license was suspended for points once before, and now Drew reaches the threshold again.

reasoning.text: A point-system suspension lasts sixty days the first time, six months the second time and twelve months the third.

result.text: Drew's second point suspension lasts six months, and at reinstatement the earlier license points are wiped out.

claim.text: Many people think reinstatement also clears insurance points.

correction.text: Reinstatement clears license points but leaves insurance points untouched, because insurers keep their own system.

prompt.text: Drew has served a second point suspension and is reinstated. Which points are wiped out?

answer.text: Every earlier driver license point; insurance points stay.

rationale.text: Reinstatement clears the license record, but insurers keep their own separate point system.

narration.text: When points cross the line, a suspension follows. This lesson covers how long point-system suspensions last, how the length grows with each repeat, what reinstatement does to the points on your record, and why your insurance company may still treat you as a risky driver even after DMV gives you a fresh start. You will also compare the clinic, which removes a few points, with reinstatement, which clears all earlier license points. These two point-removal routes are easy to confuse, and practice questions often place them side by side to see whether you can tell them apart.

A point-system suspension lasts sixty days the first time, six months the second time and twelve months the third time. Each step is a big jump. A first suspension costs about two months of driving, a second about half a year, and a third a full year. The ladder rewards drivers who learn from the first suspension and heavily penalizes those who do not. Remember that this is the adult point-system ladder. Provisional licensees under eighteen have a separate ladder based on repeat moving violations, which is covered near the end of this chapter, and its numbers are different.

When your privilege is reinstated after a suspension, every earlier driver license point is wiped out. You restart the license point count at zero. But insurance points are not affected. Insurance companies set rates with their own separate point system, and your insurance agent can answer questions about it. So the DMV record gets a fresh start, while your insurance premiums may still reflect the violations that led to the suspension. Two separate systems, kept by two separate organizations, track your driving history, and reinstatement only resets one of them.

Here is the trap. There are two ways license points come off your record, and they work very differently. Completing the clinic removes three points, whereas reinstatement after a suspension cancels every earlier license point. Neither touches insurance points. Practice questions sometimes claim the clinic wipes the record clean, or that reinstatement removes only three points. Both swap the effects. A second trap is to claim reinstatement clears insurance points too. It does not, because insurers keep their own point system. Hold the line: license points wiped, insurance stays.

Here is a quick check: Drew has just finished a second point-system suspension, which lasted six months, and the privilege is now reinstated. Which points are wiped out, and which remain? Work it out before reading on. Every earlier driver license point is wiped out, so Drew restarts the license count at zero. But insurance points are not affected, because insurance companies keep their own separate point system. Drew's insurance agent is the person to ask about rates. And Drew should remember that after reinstatement, only eight points within three years can bring another suspension.

lines.text: Sixty days, six months, twelve months.

narration.text: To wrap up, the adult point-system suspension ladder runs sixty days the first time, six months the second time and twelve months the third. When the privilege is reinstated, every earlier driver license point is wiped out, but insurance points are not affected, because insurance companies set rates with their own point system that your agent can explain. The clinic removes three points, while reinstatement removes every earlier license point. Next, we look at how many points individual violations carry on the regular point schedule.

why_how.text: Points reflect danger, so the offenses most likely to hurt someone carry the most points.
Every moving violation carries at least some points, so even small habits add up on the record.

scenario.text: Sam runs a red light and, a few months later, is convicted of tailgating.

reasoning.text: Running a red light carries three points, and tailgating carries four points.

result.text: Sam now has seven points, enough for DMV to require the driver improvement clinic.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking speeding in a school zone carries the same five points as passing a stopped school bus.

correction.text: Speeding above a posted school zone limit carries three points; five points belong to passing a stopped school bus and aggressive driving.

prompt.text: Sam is convicted of running a red light and later of tailgating. How many points has Sam collected?

answer.text: Seven points: three for the red light and four for tailgating.

rationale.text: A red light carries three points and tailgating four, which together reach the clinic threshold.

narration.text: Now that you know what point totals mean, this lesson shows how many points individual violations carry in a regular vehicle. The schedule runs from five points at the top down to one point at the bottom. The pattern is not random. The offenses most likely to injure someone, especially children and vulnerable road users, carry the most points. You do not need to memorize every line, but you should know the five-point offenses, the main four-point and three-point groups, the two-point default for other moving violations, and the single one-point offense that surprises many people.

lines.text: Five: passing a stopped school bus, aggressive driving.
Four: illegal passing, reckless driving, tailgating.
Four: property-damage hit and run, wrong side.

narration.text: In a regular vehicle, passing a stopped school bus and aggressive driving each carry five points, the highest values on the regular schedule. Next come the four-point offenses. Illegal passing, reckless driving, tailgating, which means following too closely, a property-damage-only hit and run, and driving on the wrong side of the road each carry four points. These are behaviors that put other people in immediate danger, which is why they sit near the top. A stopped school bus with children nearby is the clearest example of why the very highest value is reserved for it.

lines.text: Fail to yield to pedestrians or cyclists: four.
Stop sign, red light, failure to yield: three.
Over fifty-five miles per hour: three.

narration.text: Failing to yield to a pedestrian under the cited statute, or to a bicycle, motor scooter or motorcycle, carries four points, because those road users have little protection. A general failure to yield right of way carries three points. So do running a stop sign, running a red light, and speeding faster than fifty-five miles per hour. Notice the difference between the two yielding values. Failing to yield to a vulnerable road user is worth four points, while an ordinary failure to yield to another car is worth three. The extra point reflects how badly a pedestrian or cyclist can be hurt.

lines.text: No license, or expired over a year.
Ignoring a siren, a safety zone, no insurance.
No accident report; school zone speeding.

narration.text: Several other offenses also carry three points. Driving with no license, or with one expired over a year, ignoring a siren, driving through a safety zone, and having no liability insurance each carry three points. Failing to file a required accident report, and speeding above a posted school zone limit, each carry three points too. That last one deserves a second look. Speeding in a school zone is a three-point offense, not a five-point one. The five points near schools belong to passing a stopped school bus, which is a different and more dangerous act.

lines.text: Passing a stopped school bus: five.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two offenses involve schools, and they carry different points. Speeding above a posted school zone limit carries three points. Passing a stopped school bus carries five points in a regular vehicle, the highest on the regular schedule. Practice questions often blend these, offering five points for school zone speeding. Keep them apart. A school zone limit governs how fast you drive past a school. A stopped school bus is loading or unloading children, and passing it is one of the most dangerous moves a driver can make. The memory line: school bus and aggression, five.

Here is a quick check: Sam is convicted of running a red light, and a few months later is convicted of tailgating, following another car too closely. How many points has Sam collected? Work it out before reading on. The answer is seven points. Running a red light carries three points, and tailgating carries four. Seven is also the total at which DMV may send a driver to the driver improvement clinic. So two fairly common violations can bring a clinic notice. One more four-point offense would put Sam within reach of the twelve-point suspension line.

lines.text: Four and three: the big middle.

narration.text: To recap the regular schedule, passing a stopped school bus and aggressive driving carry five points. Illegal passing, reckless driving, tailgating, a property-damage hit and run, wrong-side driving, and failing to yield to a pedestrian, bicycle, scooter or motorcycle carry four. Stop signs, red lights, failure to yield, speeding over fifty-five, no license, ignoring a siren, safety zones, no insurance, missing accident reports and school zone speeding carry three. Child restraint violations and other unlisted moving violations carry two, and littering with a vehicle carries one.

why_how.text: Commercial vehicles are bigger and carry more people and cargo, so the same mistakes carry more points.
Not every conviction adds points; equipment, size and parking offenses are handled without them.

scenario.text: Jesse drives a commercial bus and passes a school bus that is stopped with its red lights flashing.

reasoning.text: In a commercial motor vehicle, passing a stopped school bus carries eight points, and the fine may be doubled.

result.text: Jesse gets eight points, three more than the same offense in a regular car, and may face a doubled fine.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every offense in a commercial vehicle carries high points, even littering.

correction.text: Passing a stopped school bus carries eight commercial points and a rail crossing violation six, yet littering with a vehicle still carries only one.

prompt.text: Jesse, driving a commercial bus, passes a stopped school bus. How many points apply, and what may happen to the fine?

answer.text: Eight points, and the fine may be charged double.

rationale.text: The commercial schedule gives this offense eight points, and point offenses in commercial vehicles may carry double fines.

lines.text: Higher points behind a commercial wheel.

narration.text: This lesson covers two edges of the point system. The first edge is the commercial motor vehicle schedule, where the same mistakes can carry more points because the vehicles are larger and carry passengers and cargo. The second edge is the list of offenses that add no points at all, even though they are still violations. You will also learn how fines can change when a point offense happens in a commercial vehicle. Even if you never drive a truck or bus, these rules can appear on the knowledge test, especially the comparison between regular and commercial values.

lines.text: Passing a stopped school bus: eight.

narration.text: While operating a commercial motor vehicle, passing a stopped school bus carries eight points, compared with five points in a regular vehicle. In a commercial motor vehicle, a rail-highway crossing violation and aggressive driving each carry six points. These are the highest values anywhere on North Carolina's schedules. They target the moments when a large vehicle can cause the most harm: near children getting on or off a bus, at railroad tracks, and in aggressive driving where a heavy vehicle's size and weight multiply the danger to everyone around it.

lines.text: Red light: four; other moves: three.
Alcohol in the passenger area: four.

narration.text: Other commercial values follow. In a commercial motor vehicle, reckless driving carries five points, running a red light four points, and any other moving violation three points. Having an alcoholic beverage in the passenger area of a commercial motor vehicle carries four points. Compare these with the regular schedule. Reckless driving goes from four to five, a red light from three to four, and the default for other moving violations from two to three. The commercial schedule generally sits one step higher, with the biggest jumps reserved for school buses, rail crossings and aggression.

Here is the trap. Because the commercial schedule runs higher, learners sometimes assume every offense in a commercial vehicle carries big points. Not so. On the commercial schedule, passing a stopped school bus carries eight points and a rail-highway crossing violation six, yet littering with a vehicle still carries only one point. So the vehicle type raises the values for dangerous driving, not for every offense. If a practice question asks about littering from a truck, the answer is still one point. Save the eight and the six for the school bus and the railroad crossing.

Some convictions add no points at all. Overload, overlength, overwidth and overheight convictions add no points, and neither does illegal parking. Plate, registration, muffler, emblem and inspection-certificate offenses, and carrying a concealed weapon, also add no points. These can still bring fines or other penalties, but they do not move the point total toward the clinic or a suspension. So when a question asks how many points an expired inspection sticker or a parking ticket carries, the answer is none. Points are reserved mainly for how a vehicle is driven.

lines.text: Point offense in a commercial vehicle.

narration.text: There is one more commercial rule, and it is about money rather than points. A point-carrying offense committed in a commercial motor vehicle may be charged double any fine or penalty the statute authorizes. So a commercial driver who commits a point offense can face both a higher point value and a doubled fine. Together, those rules make it very costly to drive a commercial vehicle carelessly. The logic is the same as the higher points: the larger the vehicle and its load, the greater the harm a single mistake can cause on a public road.

lines.text: Commercial bus passes a stopped school bus.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Jesse is driving a commercial bus and passes a school bus that is stopped to let children off. How many points apply, and what may happen to the fine? Work it out before reading on. The answer is eight points, and the fine may be charged double. Passing a stopped school bus carries eight points in a commercial motor vehicle, three more than the five points in a regular car, and a point-carrying offense in a commercial vehicle may be charged double the authorized fine. This is one of the most serious violations on any schedule.

lines.text: Eight for a school bus pass.
Six for rail crossings and aggression.
No points for size, parking, equipment.

narration.text: To finish, in a commercial motor vehicle passing a stopped school bus carries eight points, a rail-highway crossing violation and aggressive driving six, reckless driving five, a red light four, alcohol in the passenger area four, and other moving violations three. Littering with a vehicle still carries one point. Overload and other size offenses, illegal parking, and plate, registration, muffler, emblem, inspection and concealed weapon offenses add no points. And a point offense in a commercial vehicle may be charged double the authorized fine.

why_how.text: Some convictions take the driving privilege directly, on top of points and court penalties.
High speed and racing are singled out because they turn ordinary mistakes into deadly crashes.

scenario.text: Taylor is caught driving seventy-two in a fifty-five zone and, ten months later, seventy-five in a fifty-five zone.

reasoning.text: More than fifteen over the limit while going faster than fifty-five brings at least thirty days, and a second such charge within one year brings sixty days.

result.text: Taylor's second charge brings a sixty-day revocation.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every high-speed revocation is thirty days, no matter the history.

correction.text: One such charge brings at least thirty days, but a second within a year, or speeding with reckless driving, brings sixty days.

prompt.text: Taylor has a second charge within a year for going more than fifteen over the limit above fifty-five. How long is the revocation?

rationale.text: A second such charge within one year raises the revocation from at least thirty days to sixty.

lines.text: Some convictions skip the point count.
Speed and racing lead the list.

narration.text: Points are only one route to a suspension. On top of any criminal penalty from the court, conviction of certain traffic offenses takes away your driving privilege directly. This lesson covers the speeding and racing grounds. You will learn which speeding records let DMV suspend, how willful racing is treated, the other suspension grounds involving court orders and very high speeds, and the two specific revocation lengths for driving far over the limit at highway speeds. The numbers here are among the most tested in the chapter, so take them slowly and keep them separate.

lines.text: Two over-fifty-five convictions in twelve months.
Or one plus a reckless driving conviction.

narration.text: DMV can suspend your license for two speeding convictions over fifty-five miles per hour within twelve months, or for one over-fifty-five speeding conviction plus one reckless driving conviction within a year. A conviction for willful racing against another vehicle also lets DMV suspend, whether the race was planned ahead or not. DMV can also suspend when a court sentence orders you not to drive for a set time, and in certain cases after a conviction for speeding over seventy-five miles per hour. So high speed and racing are the main themes, along with direct court orders.

lines.text: More than fifteen over the limit.

narration.text: Driving more than fifteen miles per hour over the limit while going faster than fifty-five miles per hour brings a revocation of at least thirty days. Both conditions matter. The speed must be above fifty-five, and it must be more than fifteen over the posted limit. So seventy-two in a fifty-five zone qualifies, because it is above fifty-five and seventeen over. Fifty in a thirty-five zone does not fit this rule, even though it is fifteen over, because it is not above fifty-five. Questions often test whether you check both conditions before choosing an answer.

lines.text: Second such charge within one year.
Or speeding plus reckless driving together.

narration.text: The revocation grows to sixty days in two situations. The first is a second over-fifty-five, more-than-fifteen-over speeding charge within one year. The second is speeding of that kind together with reckless driving on the same occasion. So a repeat within a year doubles the minimum time without a license, and adding reckless driving to the high speed does the same in a single stop. These rules target drivers who show a pattern, or who combine extreme speed with other dangerous behavior, because those drivers are the most likely to cause a serious crash.

lines.text: One charge: at least thirty days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Speeding more than fifteen over the limit above fifty-five means at least thirty days, but a second such charge within a year, or speeding plus reckless driving on one occasion, means sixty days. Practice questions often offer sixty days for a first charge, or thirty days for a repeat. Use the memory line: once thirty, twice sixty. And remember the reckless driving shortcut. A driver does not need two separate stops to reach sixty days. Very high speed combined with reckless driving at the same time is enough on its own.

lines.text: Seventy in a fifty-five, ten months later.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Taylor is charged with driving seventy-two in a fifty-five zone, and ten months later is charged with driving seventy-five in a fifty-five zone. Both are more than fifteen over the limit at speeds above fifty-five. How long is the revocation for the second charge? Work it out before reading on. The answer is sixty days. A second over-fifty-five, more-than-fifteen-over speeding charge within one year brings a sixty-day revocation, up from the at least thirty days that followed the first. Two convictions over fifty-five within twelve months also let DMV suspend.

lines.text: Two over-fifty-five in a year: suspension.

narration.text: To wrap up, certain convictions take the privilege on top of court penalties. DMV can suspend for two over-fifty-five speeding convictions within twelve months, or one plus a reckless driving conviction within a year, for willful racing planned or not, for a court order not to drive, and in certain cases for speeding over seventy-five. Driving more than fifteen over the limit above fifty-five brings at least thirty days. A second such charge within a year, or that speeding with reckless driving on the same occasion, brings sixty days.

why_how.text: The most serious driving crimes bring long suspensions, because they show a driver may be a danger to others.
Prearranged racing is singled out with three years and vehicle seizure, because it is planned, deliberate danger on public roads.

scenario.text: Casey lends a car for a prearranged highway race and is convicted along with the drivers.

reasoning.text: Prearranged racing, and watching, betting on or lending a car for it, carry a three-year suspension, and the car is seized.

result.text: Casey faces a three-year suspension, and a court may order the seized car sold at public auction.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking manslaughter while impaired carries the same one-year suspension as manslaughter.

correction.text: Manslaughter brings a one-year suspension, while manslaughter under the influence of an impairing substance brings a permanent one.

prompt.text: Casey only lent a car for a prearranged race and is convicted. Which suspension applies?

rationale.text: Lending a car for a prearranged race is treated like racing itself, with three years instead of the usual one.

narration.text: The handbook lists a set of serious offenses that bring their own suspensions. Most of them carry one year. But two stand out: manslaughter while impaired, which brings a permanent suspension, and prearranged racing, which brings three years along with seizure of the car. This lesson walks through the table. You will learn the one-year offenses, the permanent exception, the speeding-to-avoid-arrest rule, the repeat reckless driving and false pretenses rules, the racing rules, and a failure-to-yield rule tied to serious injury. Watch for the exceptions; they carry the hardest practice questions.

lines.text: Manslaughter, death by vehicle: one year.
Assault with a motor vehicle: one year.

narration.text: Manslaughter, death by vehicle and assault with a motor vehicle each bring a one-year suspension, while manslaughter while impaired brings a permanent one. Death by vehicle covers a fatal crash caused by a traffic violation, and assault with a motor vehicle covers using a vehicle to hurt someone. Impairment changes everything in the most serious case. When a driver under the influence of an impairing substance kills someone, the license is gone permanently. That one exception carries the full weight of what impaired driving can do, and it is a classic test question.

Here is the trap. Manslaughter brings a one-year suspension, while manslaughter under the influence of an impairing substance brings a permanent one. Practice questions often present impaired manslaughter and offer one year, matching the rest of the table. Do not fall for it. The word impaired, or under the influence, moves the answer to permanent. The memory line is short: impaired makes it permanent. And notice that the same theme appears elsewhere in this handbook, where impairment repeatedly turns a serious offense into a far harsher penalty.

lines.text: No stop or aid after a crash.
Refusing a breath or blood test.
Fleeing arrest at very high speed.

narration.text: Several other offenses also bring one year. Failing to stop and give aid after a crash, and willfully refusing a blood or breath alcohol test, each bring a one-year suspension. Speeding over fifty-five miles per hour and at least fifteen miles per hour over the limit while trying to avoid arrest brings a one-year suspension. Two reckless driving charges within twelve months, or trying to get a license or learner permit under false pretenses, each bring a one-year suspension too. So one year is the standard in this table, and only a few offenses go higher.

lines.text: Racing, watching, betting, lending a car.

narration.text: Prearranged highway racing, and watching, betting on or lending a car for it, carry a three-year suspension. The officer seizes the car, and after conviction a court may order it sold at public auction. Notice how wide the net is. It is not only the drivers. A spectator, a bettor, or a person who lends a car for the race faces the same three years. Compare this with willful racing that was not prearranged, which lets DMV suspend the license. The planning and the crowd around a prearranged race are what raise the stakes so sharply.

Here is the second trap. Prearranged racing and helping with it carry three years, three times the one-year period for most other offenses in the same table. Practice questions sometimes give one year for racing, matching the rest of the list, or claim that people who only watched or lent a car face no suspension. Both are wrong. Remember that racing triples the year, and that the net includes spectators, bettors and lenders. A permanent suspension, meanwhile, is reserved for impaired manslaughter, so do not mix the two exceptions together.

lines.text: Casey lent a car for a race.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Casey did not drive in a prearranged highway race, but Casey lent a car to one of the racers and is convicted along with the drivers. Which suspension applies to Casey? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a three-year suspension. Prearranged racing, and watching, betting on or lending a car for it, all carry three years, three times the usual one year in the table. The officer seizes the racing car, and after conviction a court may order it sold at public auction. Lending the car was enough.

To finish, manslaughter, death by vehicle, assault with a motor vehicle, failing to stop and give aid, refusing an alcohol test, fleeing arrest at very high speed, two reckless driving charges in twelve months, and seeking a license under false pretenses each bring one year. Manslaughter while impaired brings a permanent suspension. Prearranged racing, including watching, betting or lending a car, brings three years and seizure of the car. And a failure to yield in the listed situations that causes serious bodily injury brings ninety days and five hundred dollars.

why_how.text: A driver facing revocation has a path to be heard, first at DMV and then in court.
Unpaid tickets and missed court dates can cost a license, but the court offers relief for drivers who cannot pay.

scenario.text: Morgan misses a court date for a speeding ticket and receives a revocation notice from DMV.

reasoning.text: Morgan cannot afford the ticket, so Morgan files the Motion for Relief with the clerk in the county where the ticket was issued and asks for a hearing.

result.text: The judge may lower the amount, set a payment plan or waive it, and the court notifies DMV.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a revoked driver goes straight to Superior Court.

correction.text: A revoked driver first asks DMV for a hearing; only if that fails is the appeal taken to the county Superior Court within thirty days.

prompt.text: Morgan missed a court date on a ticket and cannot afford to pay it. What should Morgan do to avoid the revocation?

answer.text: File the Motion for Relief with the clerk in the ticket's county and ask for a hearing.

rationale.text: A driver who cannot pay asks the judge for relief, and the court then notifies DMV.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens around a suspension: when DMV can act, how a driver can challenge a revocation, how convictions in other states are treated, and what happens when a ticket goes unpaid or a court date is missed. You will learn the hearing and appeal route, the written notice for out-of-state convictions, the revocation that follows missed court or unpaid fines, and the two ways to resolve a ticket, depending on whether you can pay. These procedures matter in real life too, because acting quickly on a notice can keep a license from being revoked.

lines.text: Suspension when the conviction report arrives.
Hearing in your home judicial district.
Appeal within thirty days to Superior Court.

narration.text: DMV may suspend your privilege as soon as it receives the conviction report from the court. A revoked driver may have a right to a hearing in the judicial district where they live. The handbook explains how to request one, and DMV mails you the time and place. If the hearing does not help, you may appeal the DMV decision within thirty days to the Superior Court of your home county. So the challenge route has two steps, and the second step has a firm deadline. Missing those thirty days can close the door on the appeal entirely.

lines.text: Then: Superior Court within thirty days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Practice questions sometimes describe a revoked driver heading straight to court, or appealing first and asking for a hearing later. The order is fixed. A revoked driver first asks DMV for a hearing, and only if that fails is the appeal taken to the county Superior Court within thirty days. The hearing is the first chance to fix the problem, and the court is the backstop. If an option skips the hearing or reverses the order, it is wrong. Keep the memory line in mind: hearing first, then appeal, within thirty days.

lines.text: Treated as if they happened here.

narration.text: Driving outside North Carolina does not create a loophole. A conviction in another state can lead to suspension or revocation of your North Carolina license as though it happened here, and DMV must notify you in writing of the effective date. So a reckless driving conviction on a trip to another state can count just as if it had happened at home. When you receive such a notice, the same hearing and appeal route applies. Practice questions that claim out-of-state convictions never affect a North Carolina license are testing exactly this rule.

lines.text: Avoided if paid or waived first.
Paying does not erase a conviction.

narration.text: If you miss court or do not pay a fine for a citation, DMV sets a revocation date. It takes effect unless the fine is paid or waived first, and it lasts until the court reports payment or waiver. There is an important limit, though. Taking care of the citation does not cancel the consequences of the offense itself if you are convicted. Paying stops the revocation for nonpayment, but points and any other penalties from the conviction still follow. So paying a ticket resolves the money problem, not the driving record that the offense created.

title.text: Two ways to resolve a ticket

lines.text: Cannot pay: Motion for Relief and a hearing.
Can pay: pay the clerk in full.
Either way, the court tells DMV.

narration.text: There are two routes, depending on your situation. If you cannot afford a ticket, you file the Motion for Relief form with the clerk in the county where you got the ticket and ask for a hearing. The judge may lower the amount, set a payment plan or waive it. If you can pay in full, you contact the clerk in that county, pay the whole amount, and the court tells DMV, which stops the suspension. In both routes, the court notifies DMV. So the clerk in the ticket's county is always your starting point, not DMV. Relief comes from the judge, never from DMV.

Here is a quick check: Morgan missed a court date for a speeding ticket, and DMV has set a revocation date. Morgan cannot afford to pay the fine. What should Morgan do to avoid the revocation? Work it out before reading on. Morgan should file the Motion for Relief form with the clerk in the county where the ticket was issued and ask for a hearing. The judge may lower the amount, set a payment plan or waive it, and the court notifies DMV. Even then, if Morgan is convicted, the offense's own consequences still apply.

Let us recap. DMV may suspend as soon as it receives the conviction report, and a revoked driver may request a hearing in their home judicial district, then appeal within thirty days to the home county Superior Court if the hearing fails. Out-of-state convictions count as though they happened here, with written notice of the effective date. Missed court or unpaid fines lead to a revocation date unless paid or waived first. Drivers who cannot pay file a Motion for Relief, drivers who can pay pay the clerk in full, and paying never erases a conviction's consequences.

why_how.text: Teen drivers face a faster suspension ladder, because repeat violations early in a driving life signal serious risk.
Getting a license back takes fees and paperwork, so a suspension costs money as well as time.

scenario.text: Avery, a sixteen-year-old provisional licensee, is convicted of a third moving violation within twelve months.

reasoning.text: A provisional licensee faces ninety days for a third and six months for a fourth moving violation within twelve months.

result.text: Avery is suspended for ninety days, then pays the restoration fee and completes the steps at a license office.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking provisional drivers follow the adult sixty-day, six-month, twelve-month ladder.

correction.text: For a provisional licensee the ladder runs thirty days, ninety days and six months, counted from the second, third and fourth moving violation within twelve months.

prompt.text: Avery is sixteen and gets a third moving violation conviction within twelve months. How long is the suspension?

rationale.text: The provisional ladder is thirty days for a second, ninety for a third and six months for a fourth violation within twelve months.

lines.text: A faster ladder for provisional drivers.

narration.text: This final lesson in the chapter has two parts. First, the special suspension ladder for provisional licensees, the young drivers you met in the graduated licensing chapter. Their suspensions are counted from repeat moving violations rather than from points, and the ladder starts sooner than the adult one. Second, what everyone must do to get a license back after a suspension or revocation: the restoration fees, the higher fee after a DWI, the service fee and how to avoid it, and the steps at a driver license office. Both parts are full of numbers, so go slowly.

lines.text: Second violation in twelve months: thirty days.

narration.text: A provisional licensee under eighteen faces a thirty-day suspension for a second moving violation conviction within twelve months. A provisional licensee faces ninety days for a third and six months for a fourth moving violation conviction within twelve months. Notice that the first violation does not trigger a suspension on this ladder; the count starts with the second. And notice the twelve-month window, much shorter than the three-year point window for adults. Young drivers with several violations in a single year are showing a pattern the state wants to interrupt quickly.

lines.text: Adult points: sixty, six months, twelve.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two suspension ladders exist, and practice questions love to swap them. For a provisional licensee the ladder runs thirty days, ninety days and six months, counted from the second, third and fourth moving violation within twelve months. The adult point-system ladder runs sixty days, then six months, then twelve months, counted from point suspensions. So if the driver is a provisional licensee with repeat moving violations, use thirty, ninety, six months. If the driver is an adult crossing point thresholds, use sixty days, six months, twelve months. Read who the driver is first.

lines.text: Not charged after a medical evaluation.

narration.text: Clearing a suspension or revocation requires a restoration fee of eighty-three dollars and fifty cents, except when the license was taken for medical reasons after a medical evaluation. Restoring after a DWI revocation costs more: one hundred sixty-seven dollars and twenty-five cents. A fifty dollar service fee also applies, unless you surrendered the license to the court or mailed it to DMV before the effective date. So acting promptly on a revocation notice, by surrendering or mailing in the license on time, saves money later. Fees can change, so check current amounts when the time comes.

lines.text: Visit a license office and prove identity.
Tests, insurance proof, new license fee.

narration.text: To get your privilege back, you go to a driver license office, prove your identity, pay the fees, reapply, take any required tests, show insurance if required, and pay for the new license. So restoration is close to applying all over again. The restoration fee is only part of the cost, because the new license has its own fee, and insurance proof may be needed, as the insurance lesson explained. Planning for each step, including printed insurance proof less than thirty days old, makes the trip to the office go smoothly and gets you driving legally again.

Here is a quick check: Avery is a sixteen-year-old provisional licensee who has just been convicted of a third moving violation within twelve months. How long is the suspension? Work it out before reading on. The answer is ninety days. The provisional ladder runs thirty days for a second, ninety days for a third and six months for a fourth moving violation within twelve months. Avery should not reach for the adult numbers of sixty days or six months. After the ninety days, Avery pays the restoration fee and completes the steps at a license office.

To finish the chapter, a provisional licensee under eighteen faces thirty days for a second, ninety days for a third and six months for a fourth moving violation conviction within twelve months. Getting a license back requires a restoration fee of eighty-three dollars and fifty cents, except after a medical evaluation, while a DWI restoration costs one hundred sixty-seven dollars and twenty-five cents, plus a fifty dollar service fee unless the license was surrendered or mailed in first. Then visit a license office, prove identity, pay, reapply, test, show insurance and pay for the new license.
